question: A communications officer pastes a ten-page partner agreement into the chat and types her instructions directly underneath it, with nothing marking where the pasted document ends and her request begins. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The conversation will become too long to continue, so she will have to start the whole exchange again shortly.
B) The signed agreement will be reformatted as it is pasted, so its clauses arrive in a different order from the original.
C) Claude will answer only from the closing paragraphs, because material earlier in a long message is set aside.
D) Claude may read wording inside the agreement as directions to follow, and act on it instead of her actual request.
correct_answers: D) Claude may read wording inside the agreement as directions to follow, and act on it instead of her actual request.
explanations: A ten-page agreement is well within what a single chat handles, and length is a separate concern from failing to separate instructions from source material.
Some layout is lost when text is pasted, but clause order is preserved, and reordering is not what makes an unlabelled paste risky.
Claude works from the whole message rather than only its final paragraphs, so this misstates how a long pasted document is handled.

Correct. Contracts contain imperative language such as 'the supplier shall notify' or 'provide a summary within ten days'. With no boundary between the pasted material and her instructions, that wording can be taken as part of the task, and the output drifts away from what she asked for.
